reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
story:
Amelia held a book about turtles. It had a shiny green cover. She opened it and saw little black marks on every page.

"What are these?" she asked. Her mother smiled. "Those are words. They say things."

Amelia squinted at the marks. "The turtle page says turtle things," she decided. She turned the pages from the front to the back. "This way," she said, nodding.

"I want to keep this book forever," Amelia said. She hugged it tight.

Her mother shook her head. "We borrow library books. Then we take them back. Other kids want to read about turtles too."

Amelia frowned at the turtle book. Then she frowned at the shelf. Another girl stood there, looking sad.

"Are you waiting for this book?" Amelia asked her.

The girl nodded. "Turtles are my favorite."

Amelia looked at the cover one more time. She opened the front page and pointed at the words. "The words tell turtle things," she said. "You read this way, front to back."

She gave the book to the girl. The girl waved goodbye. Amelia waved back.

"Can we come back next week?" Amelia asked her mother.

"Yes," said her mother. "And maybe the turtle book will be home again."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Scarlett wanted to help Mom make soup. Mom said, "You can watch from here." Scarlett stood on her stool.

The pot began to hiss. Steam rose up like a little cloud. Mom put in a spoon and lifted it out. "This is hot," Mom said. She blew on the spoon. She blew one time. She blew two times. Then she touched a tiny drop to her lip. "Now it is warm."

Scarlett wanted to touch the pot. Mom shook her head. "Hot things can hurt you," she said. "We look with our eyes."

Scarlett looked with her eyes. She saw the soup roll and bubble. Then Mom gave her a cool cup of water. Scarlett put her hand on it. "This one is cold!" she said. "The pot is hot. My cup is cold."

After lunch, Scarlett was tired. She climbed into her bed. Her teddy was waiting there. Mom tucked her in. "Stay close to me when you wake up," Mom said.

Scarlett nodded. "Hot pot, cold cup," she said softly. Her eyes closed. Mom smiled and turned out the light.

story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. A big bowl sat in the middle. It was too far away. "I want the peas," she said. Her tummy wanted food now. That was her problem.

"Pass the peas, please," said Daddy. Mommy passed the bowl. Then Daddy passed it to Aubrey. Lucky girl! She put her nose close. "I smell them," she said. Her nose did that. She looked at the peas. Her eyes saw little green balls. She counted them out loud. "One pea, two peas, three peas." She touched the peas with her fingers. Cold and smooth.

Then Aubrey ate one pea. Her tongue tasted it. Yum! She heard a funny sound. Crunch, crunch. Her ears heard it. "The peas go crunch," she said. "My ears heard that." She ate some more. "One pea, two peas, three peas." Mommy smiled. Aubrey smiled too. "More peas, please," she said.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Livia went to the art gallery with her dad. She saw a big red painting. "Red," she said. Dad smiled and nodded.

Then she saw a blue painting. "Blue," she said. Then a yellow one. "Yellow!" Dad clapped his hands.

At a little table there were paints. Livia wanted to make green like the grass. She painted with yellow. It was just yellow. She painted more yellow. Still just yellow. A boy next to her was sad. His brush fell down with a little noise. Livia picked it up for him. He said, "Thank you." He pointed at his paint. It was blue.

Livia had an idea. She put blue on her yellow. She mixed it with her brush. The paint turned green! "Blue and yellow make green," she said.

Dad said, "Let's try red and yellow." Livia mixed them. The paint turned orange. Then she mixed red and blue. It turned purple, not yucky at all.

A gallery lady came by. "What a pretty green," she said. Livia chased a drip of paint down the paper with her brush.

"We can hang it at home," said Dad. Livia held up her painting. "Look, green!" she said.

story:
Thomas wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He stood on his little stool by the sink. He turned the tap. The water came out. It was cold. Thomas put his hands under it. "Too cold!" he said.

Then Thomas turned the other tap. Steam floated up. Thomas held his hand close, not touching. The air felt hot. He pulled his hand back fast. "Hot water can hurt me," Thomas said. He turned the hot tap back a little. Then he mixed the two waters. He felt it with one finger. Now it was warm and nice. Thomas rubbed the rough towel on his wet hands. He did not touch the pink soap with the sharp top, because that was Mama's.

Mama came to the door. "I will not forget you, Mama," Thomas said. He held out his hand. "Can we have a cookie now?" Mama laughed and took his warm, dry hand.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Nora wanted to go outside. The sheep on her coat needed to come too. But first she had to put it on. She pushed one arm in. She pushed the other arm in. "One, two," she said.

Now the zipper. She pulled it up. But the zipper did not move. Nora pulled again. "Oh no," she said. The zipper made a loud noise, click, click. Dad looked over. "Your coat is all bumpy," he said. Nora looked down. Yes, the coat was twisted. One side was up and one side was down.

Nora smoothed the coat. She made it flat. She made it straight. Then she held the zipper and pulled. Up it went! "Zip it all the way to the sheep," said Dad. Nora zipped it to the top. She patted the sheep. "Bumpy coat, no zip," Nora said. "Flat coat, yes zip!" She ran to the door. "Outside now!"

story:
Miles went to the library with his dad. They rode the bus. The bus was not heavy to sit on, but the doors were heavy to push.

Miles wanted to draw on the library tablet. He pushed the button on top. The screen stayed dark. He held the button down and counted. One, two, three. The screen lit up. "It comes on when I hold it," said Miles. He tapped the little paint pot. The drawing app opened. He drew a big red cat.

Then it was time to go. Miles did not just set the tablet down. He tapped the app closed. He held the button again and the screen went dark. He hung his picture on the fridge later. "Hold the button, draw, then put it away," said Miles. His dad smiled and held his hand.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Cooper wanted the red car. His big sister Mia wanted it too. She grabbed one end. He grabbed the other end. The car did not go anywhere.

Then Mia said, "You go first. Then me." She let go. Cooper zoomed the car on the floor. One turn. Two turns. Then he gave the car to Mia. She zoomed it too. It was fair.

Outside, rain fell on the street. The road was wet. Cooper watched from the window. He saw a man slip on the wet street. The man got up slow. He walked on, more careful now.

"The floor is wet too," Cooper said. He walked with small steps. The car was safe in his hands. Mia held out her hand. Cooper put the car in it.

"Your turn," he said.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Sara went to the library with her Mama. The library sat next to the bread store. Sara could smell the warm bread. She felt happy.

Sara wanted the big red book about wild bears. She ran to the shelf. Her heart went fast. She was so excited. Then a shelf fell over. CRASH! Sara jumped. Her tummy felt tight. She was scared.

Mama knelt down next to her. "Take a big breath," Mama said. "Breathe in slow." Sara breathed in slow. Then she breathed out. Her tummy felt loose again. "The loud noise made me scared," Sara said. "The slow breath made me feel better." Then Sara saw a little boy crying by the fallen shelf. His book was under it. He looked sad. Sara picked up the book and gave it to him. He stopped crying. He smiled a big smile. Sara smiled too. "Mama," she said, "I helped him." Mama hugged her tight.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Charlie wanted toast with butter all by herself. She took the butter out of the fridge. The butter was cold and hard. She pushed it on the bread. The bread tore. "Oh no," said Charlie.

Then the butter sat on the counter while she got her cup. The butter got warm and soft. She tried again. The soft butter made the toast smooth. It went on thin, like a little blanket. "Why did it work now?" Charlie asked herself. "The butter got warm. Warm butter is soft!" She put a small pat on top. It looked like a little yellow flower.

Next came the milk. Charlie set the cup on the table. She held the jug with two hands. She poured slowly, slowly. One step, two steps, three steps, pour. The milk went up, up, up. Not one drop spilled.

"Look, Mama!" said Charlie. "I made breakfast all by myself." She took a big bite of toast and a big sip of milk. "Can we do it again tomorrow?"

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
story:
Madeline was at Grandma's house. It was her birthday. Big balloons sat on the chair. The cake came out. It had three little candles on top. The candles were lit. They made little flames.

Madeline wanted to eat the cake. She reached for it. "Wait," said Grandma. "The candles are still on." Madeline looked at the flames. They were warm. She could feel the heat on her nose.

Grandpa leaned down. "Make a wish," he said. "Then blow." Madeline took a big breath. She blew hard. Out went the candles. One, two, three. Little smoke curls went up. They looked like gray ribbons.

"Now we can eat," said Grandma. The cake was cool and sweet. Frosting got on Madeline's nose. Her friend Sam laughed. Grandma wiped Sam's chin with a soft napkin. Grandpa gave everyone milk. Madeline sat on the big chair and took another bite.

"The candles made it hot," said Madeline. "I blew them out. Now it's cake time." Everyone clapped. Madeline blew a kiss at the empty candles.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard with Dad.

"Stay close," said Dad. Maria stayed close to Dad.

Then Maria saw the grill. The grill made a little smoke. She wanted to touch it.

"Hot," said Dad. "We do not touch the grill."

Maria stopped her hand. She found a stick. She held the stick near the grill. The stick got warm. Then the stick got hot. Maria dropped the stick on the grass.

"Hot," said Maria. "The fire makes it hot."

She wiped her hands on her hat. Then she went to the cold water bucket. Maria put one finger in the water. "Cold," she said. She put both hands in. The cold water felt good on her warm fingers.

Dad sat down on the bench. Maria sat right next to him. "I stay close," said Maria.

"You stay close," said Dad. "Good girl."

Maria watched the smoke go up, up, up. Her new hat kept the sun off her head. She waited with Dad until the corn was ready. It smelled so good.

"Cold hands, warm corn," said Maria, and she smiled.

story:
Alice went to the store with her brother. They wanted apples for snack time. Alice was hungry already.

Mum said, "We need ten apples." Alice put apples in a basket. One, two, three. Then the basket tipped over. Apples rolled on the floor. "Oh no," said Alice.

Her brother knelt down with her. They tried to pick up every apple. Alice counted as they went. "One, two, three, four, five." Her brother found one more under the shelf. "Six!" Alice held up an apple. "Seven, eight, nine." They looked and looked. One apple was still missing.

Then Alice saw it. It had rolled to the big orange pumpkins. She picked it up. "Ten!" she said. "All the apples came back."

Mum smiled. "Why did they roll so far?" she asked.

Alice thought. "The floor is smooth," she said. "Smooth things roll fast."

She put the ten apples in the basket. She held the basket with both hands this time. Her brother carried the bread. Alice counted the apples one more time on the way home. "Ten apples for our snack," she said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Lydia skipped all the way to the big stadium. She held Daddy's hand. "One, two, three, up we go," Daddy said as they climbed the steps.

The game began. Lydia sat in her seat. Then everyone stood up and waved. Tall people were all around her. Lydia could not see the game. Her tummy felt sad. She pulled Daddy's sleeve. "Too many feet," she said. Daddy looked down at her. Then he smiled and lifted her up on his shoulders.

Now Lydia was taller than everyone. "One, two, three, I can see!" she said. She clapped her hands. The crowd roared. Lydia waved her little flag. A man scored a goal. Everyone jumped. Lydia bounced on Daddy's shoulders. At last she saw the whole game, from way up high. "I see it because I am up," Lydia said. Daddy laughed. "Yes, you are," he said. "Wave your flag one more time."

story:
Emilia went to the store with Mama. She saw a big red balloon. Emilia wanted the balloon for her friend Sam's present. But a boy was holding it. He was crying because his mama said it was time to go.

The boy put the balloon down. Emilia picked it up. Then she saw the boy still crying. He wanted it too. Emilia thought hard. She looked at the balloon. She looked at the boy.

"Here," Emilia said. "You take it first. Then it is my turn." The boy smiled and held the balloon. He gave it back to Emilia after one minute. Emilia counted the minute out loud, slow and deep, like a big drum. Then she hugged the balloon. At the store, the man at the door said, "One line, one turn, everyone waits." Emilia waited in the line. She got her turn. She paid with coins from Mama.

At home, Emilia gave Sam the balloon. "We took turns," she said. Sam squeezed it tight and laughed.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Chloe wanted to play the senses game. Mom said, "Name five senses, and win a star."

Chloe held a red apple. "I see it with my eyes," she said. Then she sniffed it. "I smell it with my nose." Mom clapped.

Chloe stopped. "What comes next?" Mom put the apple by Chloe's back. "No fair!" said Chloe. "My ears can't see it!" She turned around and grinned.

She bit the apple. "Crunchy! I taste it with my mouth." Then she touched her teddy bear. "Soft! I touch with my hands."

Mom held up the star. "Five senses, five body parts. You did it!" Chloe hugged the bear. "My hands feel squishy teddy!" she said, and took another big crunchy bite.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
story:
Andrew went to the little pool by the lake. He wanted to swim like the big kids. But Andrew felt shy. He sat at the edge and watched.

Dad held his hand. "Try one little kick," Dad said. Andrew held the rail. He put his face in the water. He blew out with his mouth. Bubbles came up. Pop, pop, pop! Andrew lifted his head. He laughed. "The bubbles pop because I blow," he said.

He tried again. He blew more air. More bubbles came. More bubbles popped. Then Andrew let his feet float up behind him. His legs did not sink. They sat on top of the water like a boat. "Dad, look! My feet come up when I blow!" Dad smiled and held him steady. After all that blowing, Andrew was tired. They lay on the towel in the sun. Andrew took a little nap. When he woke up, he said, "More bubbles now, please."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Chloe stood on her stool at the kitchen wall. She had toast and a butter knife. She wanted to do it all by herself.

She pushed the knife hard. The butter was cold and hard. The toast tore. A big hole! Chloe laughed. "Oops. Toast boat." Dad put a new slice in the toaster. He set the butter dish near the warm toaster. Soon the butter went soft and shiny. Chloe slid her knife across it. The soft butter spread like paint. "Soft butter goes on easy!" she said. "Cold butter makes holes."

Then came the milk. Chloe held the little jug with two hands. She poured too fast. Milk slipped down the side and made a puddle. She got a cloth and wiped it up. Then she tried again, very slow, like a sleepy turtle. Drip. Drip. Drip. Not one drop spilled.

"Look, Dad!" said Chloe. "Slow milk stays in the cup." Dad clapped. "Big girl milk," he said. "Stormy clouds outside, but our kitchen is dry." Chloe drank her milk and ate her buttery toast, every bite, even the crumbs.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
story:
Emilia ran into the clinic. She was first in line for her turn. She loved the doctor, but not shots.

"Nurse Amy, will the shot hurt?" she asked.

"A little," said Nurse Amy. "But try this. Let your arm go soft and loose."

Emilia squeezed her arm tight. It felt like a rock. Then she tried. She let her arm go soft. She wiggled her fingers and counted to three.

"One, two, three."

The needle went in. It was just a quick pinch!

"That was small!" Emilia said. "My arm was tight before. Tight made it hurt more. Soft made it hurt less!"

Nurse Amy put a band aid on. Emilia held up her arm.

"My arm feels a little weak," she said, "but it is still strong enough for a sticker!"

She picked a shiny star and held it high.

story:
Henry ran to the park. He heard a bell ring. Ding, ding, ding! Henry used his ears to hear it. "The ice cream truck!" he said. But where was it?

Henry looked with his eyes. He could not see the truck. He turned his head all the way. There it was! "My eyes see it!" said Henry. The truck stopped by the sandbox. Henry dug in the sand. He made a big, round hole. "Look! An ocean!" he said.

The man held out ice cream. Henry sniffed with his nose. It smelled sweet. He licked it with his tongue. Yum! It tasted cold and yummy. A dog ran by. "Phew, that dog is smelly," said Henry. Henry patted the dog with his hand. The fur felt soft.

Henry sat on the bench. The dog sat too. "We can talk with our mouths," said Henry. He licked his ice cream again. "More tomorrow!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Henry went to the library with Mom. Today was story time. Yesterday, the library had a cake party. Henry had licked the frosting off his piece. It was the last cake on the plate.

Henry looked at the big table. "Where is the cake?" he asked. Mom smiled softly. "The cake was yesterday," she said. "Today we have story time. The cake is all gone."

Henry frowned a little. He wanted cake now. "Can we get cake now?" he asked. "Not now," said Mom. "Later we can bake one at home." Henry touched the empty table with his hand. It felt smooth and cool. "The cake is gone because yesterday is done," he said.

Then the librarian rang a little bell. Story time was starting now. Henry sat down on the soft rug. He picked a book about a red truck. "Can we read the truck book tomorrow too?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Tomorrow we can come back." Henry hugged the book to his chest and turned the first page.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Hayden went to the library with Dad. He wanted a book about a big elephant. But where was it?

The books were all mixed up. He saw a book about apples. He saw a book about a teddy bear. He saw a book about a bus. No elephant anywhere.

Then Hayden saw little signs on the shelves. One sign had a cow on it. The cow shelf held cow books, pig books, and duck books. All the animals lived there!

He ran to the animal shelf. He hugged the books close to his chest. There was a blue book with a big gray elephant on the cover. It was heavy. His grip felt loose, so he held on tight.

"Look, Dad! Elephants are animals. Apples are foods. This is the animal shelf!"

Hayden sat down on a soft rug. He opened the elephant book. The pages made a swish sound. Then something fell out. It was a shiny bookmark shaped like a tiny peanut. The elephant in the picture seemed to wink at him.

"Elephants love peanuts," said Hayden. "This is for you, elephant." He put the bookmark right on the elephant's long nose.

Dad smiled. "Time to close the book soon. We can take it home."

"One more page," said Hayden. "The elephant is still hungry."

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
story:
Lincoln put on his blue coat. He went to the corner store with Dad. "Can I pick the apples?" he asked. "Yes," said Dad. "We need six."

Lincoln counted the red apples. One, two, three, four, five, six. Then he counted them the other way, starting from the other end. One, two, three, four, five, six. He frowned. It was six both times! How could that be? He counted them again, very slowly. Six again.

"The last number I say is six," said Lincoln. "So there are six." Dad smiled and put them in the bag. Then Lincoln saw two baskets of oranges. He counted one basket. Eight. He counted the small basket. Five. "This one has more," he said, pointing. He helped build a tall stack of them by the register. The stack did not fall. "Eight is more than five," said Lincoln. "Because when I count, the last number tells me."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Joshua ran into the big hall. There was a desk by the door. Grandma was sitting at the desk. She handed out spoons and cups. The sky outside was cloudy and gray.

"Time for soup," said Grandma. Joshua grabbed his spoon fast. Then everyone held hands in one big circle. "We say the blessing first," said Grandma. Joshua put his spoon down on the desk. He held Grandpa's hand and Mama's hand. Grandpa said the blessing. Joshua listened. Then everyone said, "Amen!" Joshua clapped. "Now we eat!" said Grandma. Joshua picked his spoon back up. The soup was warm and yummy.

A dog barked outside the window. "The dog wants soup too," said Grandpa. Joshua giggled. "Dogs can't hold hands," said Joshua. Grandpa laughed and laughed. "Blessing first, then soup," said Joshua, and he slurped his bowl.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Anna was at the playground. She saw the big slide. The slide looked like a dark dragon tail.

Anna wanted to go down it. But the ladder was tall. Her feet could not fit on the first step.

A boy named Sam stood by the ladder. Anna said, "Please help me climb." Sam held her hand. Up, up, up she went.

"Thank you, Sam," said Anna. At the top, Anna pretended to be a lion. "Roar! I am a lion on a mountain!"

She slid down fast. Whee! Then she bumped into Sam at the bottom. Sam fell on the grass.

"Sorry," said Anna. She helped Sam stand up. Sam smiled.

"Why did you say sorry?" Sam asked.

"Because I bumped you. Bumping hurts. Sorry makes it better," said Anna.

Sam nodded. "Want to be lions together?"

"Yes! Roar!" said Anna. Two lions ran around the playground.

Then Anna's shoe came untied. "Help, please," she called. Mama came and tied it tight.

"There," said Mama. "Now the shoe will fit just right."

"Thank you, Mama," said Anna. She roared one more time and ran to the swings.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
William went to a big festival with his grandma. There was music and food and a long table. Outside, kids ran near a playground. One boy began to fall, and William helped him up.

At the table, everyone held hands. Grandma said they would say a blessing first. William did not wait. He grabbed a sharp piece of bread and put it in his mouth. Nobody else was eating yet. William looked around. He put the bread down on his plate.

Grandma smiled at him. She squeezed his hand. Then she said the blessing, and everyone said thank you together. After that, they all ate. William tried again at the next meal. He held hands. He waited. He said the blessing with grandma, word by word.

"You waited," said grandma. William picked up his bread and took a big bite.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Blake walked on the nature trail with Dad. She wanted to know a game for the long walk. Dad said, "Let's play the five senses game." He held up one finger. "First, eyes. What do you see?" Blake saw a green leaf. "I see a leaf with my eyes!" she said.

Then Blake heard water. She pointed to her ears. "I hear the water with my ears!" Dad smiled. They came to a pine tree. Blake touched the bark. "I feel the bark with my hands!" Next she sniffed the air. "I smell pine with my nose!" One sense was left. Dad poured a sip of water from his bottle into her cup. Blake drank it. "I taste the water with my mouth!"

Just then rain began to fall. Blake felt drops on her face. "The rain is wet because water falls from the sky," she said. Dad laughed. "You used your hands and your skin. That is neat!" Blake counted on her fingers: eyes, ears, hands, nose, mouth. "Five senses," she said. "I did it!" She jumped in a small puddle with both feet.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Axel ran into his classroom. Snow was falling outside. It made a thick white coat on the window.

"Today we count!" said Miss Ana. She clapped her hands. All the children stood in a circle.

Axel wanted to count the loud drum. Miss Ana said, "When we count, we say the numbers in a row. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

Axel began. "One, two, three, five!" He hit the drum one time for each word. But there were ten crackers on the plate. The drum stopped at five. "Where did four go?" Axel asked.

Mia stood next to him. She pointed at her fingers. "Look. The words go in order. You skipped one." Axel looked at her fingers. He tapped each one as he said a word.

"One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" Ten taps. Ten crackers. All the children clapped. Miss Ana put a cracker in his hand.

Axel grinned. "The words have to stay in their line!" He ran back to the window to count the snowflakes, one by one.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Michael ran into Grandma's house. Tonight was Diwali, the festival of lights! Grandma had small clay lamps called diyas. Each one had a little cotton wick and a drop of oil.

"I want to light one!" said Michael. Grandma helped him. But when they set his diya on the porch, the wind blew. The flame went out. Michael set it out again. The wind blew it out again.

Then Michael saw Grandpa's lamp. It sat behind a big glass jar. The wind could not reach it. Michael found a jar too. He put his diya inside it. He lit the wick. The flame stood up tall. "The wind can't get it now!" he said. Grandma clapped. The pet dog barked at all the bright lights.

Soon Michael was sleepy. He fell asleep on Grandma's lap, with his little lamp still shining.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Bennett jumped into his big car seat. "Go, go, go!" he called. Daddy started the car. It went fast, then slow, then fast again.

Bennett looked out the window. A big truck went by. Vroom! A small bug sat on the glass. It was so tiny. Outside the sun was hot. Bennett touched the window. Hot, hot, hot! He touched his cold juice cup. Cold! "Hot window, cold juice," he said. Daddy laughed.

Daddy said, "We will get ice cream soon." Bennett clapped. Ice cream was yummy, yummy, yummy! They stopped at the ice cream shop. Bennett got a vanilla cone. He sat in the car and held it tight.

The sun was hot. The ice cream started to drip. Drip, drip, drip, right onto his cone. "My ice cream is melting!" said Bennett. He looked up at the hot sun. "The sun is hot. That makes it melt!" Daddy gave him a paper plate. Bennett put the cone on the plate and ate fast. "Big bites, Daddy, big bites! I will eat it all up!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandpa was coming to stay for a whole week. Violet waited by the kitchen window. Then his car pulled up. "Grandpa!" she shouted. He hugged her tight.

On day two, Grandpa sat quietly at the table. He did not eat his toast. "I miss my sheep," he said. "At home, I paint them every morning." Violet knew what to do. She found paper and her paint pots. She put them right in front of him. Grandpa picked up a brush. He painted a funny sheep with a curly face. Then he laughed and laughed and ate all his toast.

"You were sad because you missed your sheep," said Violet. "Now you painted one, so you are happy." Grandpa nodded and gave her a big kiss. Violet painted a sheep too. They painted side by side, all week long, until the paper covered the whole kitchen table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Andrew went to the park with his mom. The sun was bright. He ran to the slide. He put his hand on it. "Ow! It is hot," he said. The sun made the metal hot. He pulled his hand back fast.

"Let's wait," said Mom. They sat in the shade under a tree. Andrew heard leaves whisper over his head. He saw a snowy patch behind the fence. It felt cold when he poked it with his boot.

Then they walked past the little farm. A pink pig sat in the pen. Andrew wanted to pat it. "Stay back," said Mom. "The fence keeps us safe." Andrew waved at the pig instead. The pig wiggled its nose.

Later the sun went behind a cloud. Andrew touched the slide again. It was not hot now. He climbed up. He went down, fast and smooth. "The sun made it hot before," he said. Mom clapped. "You waited, and now you can slide."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
story:
Blake went to the library with her mama. There was a new rug by the story corner. It was blue like a lake. Blake sat down on the soft blue lake.

The teacher held up one duck puppet. "We will pass the duck," she said. Blake wanted the duck first. But a boy named Sam got it first. Sam made the duck quack. Then Sam passed the duck to Blake. Blake made the duck quack too. Then she passed it to the next kid. "Why do we pass it?" Blake asked her mama. "So everyone gets a turn," Mama said. One duck, many kids, so they took turns.

At the end, the teacher said, "We all win, because we all had a turn." Blake smiled and hugged the duck one more time. Then she put it in the basket. "Bye, duck," she said. "See you at the lake."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Iris wanted to wear her red shoes tomorrow. But she could not find them. She looked under her bed. She found one sticky candy wrapper there. "Yuck," she said. She kept looking.

"It is nighttime now," said Dad. "The shoes can wait until later. Tomorrow is not here yet." Iris sat on her bed. She did not want to wait. Waiting felt long.

Dad helped her look anyway. They looked slowly. They looked in the toy box. They looked by the door. Then Iris felt something tickle her toes inside her slipper. She wiggled her foot. Out fell a red shoe! The other red shoe was under the blanket.

"The shoes hid from me," Iris said. "I found them because I kept looking." Dad smiled and put the shoes by the door.

"Now I sleep," said Iris. "Then it will be tomorrow, and I will wear my red shoes." She pulled the blanket up to her chin and closed her eyes.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Brooklyn went to the bookshop with Dad. She wanted to find a book about bears. She looked and looked. There were so many books!

Dad pointed to a big letter on a sign. It was B. "That is B," he said. Brooklyn frowned. How would B help her?

Then she said the letter out loud. "B says buh," she said. Then she said her own name. "Brooklyn. Buh, buh, Brooklyn!" The B was at the start of her name!

She looked at the shelves again. She saw a word that began with B. She said the first sound. "Buh. Buh, bear!" The word said bear! She pulled the book out. A friendly bear smiled on the cover.

"Can you spell bear?" asked Dad. "B," said Brooklyn, proudly. "Then the other letters come after." She could not say them all yet, but she knew the first one.

"Maybe B can find more books," said Dad. Brooklyn walked along the shelf. She saw a word that began with B. "Buh, buh. Bunnies!" She found a bunny book too.

"Did B help you find them?" Dad asked. Brooklyn nodded. "Yes. B makes the buh sound. So my eyes find B first."

On the way home, they talked about dinner. "Bananas," said Brooklyn. "Bananas start with B too!" Dad laughed. Brooklyn hugged her bear book.

"Tomorrow," she said, "I want to find the letter C."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Sara dug little holes in the dirt. She dropped a seed in each hole. Then she covered the seeds with soft brown soil. "Grow, little seeds," she said. "Grow, grow." Her dog Max dug too. He hid a big bone in the corner of the garden. "Silly Max," said Sara. She patted his head.

Every day Sara watered her seeds with a small blue can. Green leaves popped up in the sun. But in the corner, by the tall wall, nothing grew. Sara waited and waited. She watered that spot too. Still nothing came up. Then she sat and watched all morning. The sun moved over the sky. The sun did not shine on the corner at all. "The seeds need sun," said Sara. "That is why they will not grow."

So Sara planted new seeds in the sunny spot. Soon the leaves grew tall there too. Tiny red tomatoes came out. "Look, Max!" said Sara. "The sun helped them grow." The sun began to sink behind the barn. Max dug up his bone and lay down in the warm grass. Sara held a pretty red tomato in her two hands. "Grow, little seeds," she whispered. "Grow, grow."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Victor wanted apple juice at snack time. Miss Ana held the big jug. Victor reached and grabbed. Miss Ana said, "Please ask with words." Victor said, "Please pour me juice." Miss Ana smiled. She pour, pour, poured the juice into his cup. "Thank you," said Victor. "You are welcome," said Miss Ana.

Victor took his cup with both hands. But his sock slipped on the floor. The cup tipped. Juice went splash, splash, splash. Victor felt his face go hot. "Sorry," he said to Miss Ana. "It slipped out of my hands." Miss Ana knelt down. "Accidents happen," she said. "Let's clean it up together." One towel, two towels, three towels. They wiped the floor till it was dry.

Then Miss Ana helped him pour a new cup, just a little bit. "Little cups do not tip," she said. Victor held it with both hands. He did not spill one drop. "Please works," said Victor. "I asked, and you helped me."

After snack, the class made red paper fire for their pretend fire truck. Victor glued on one flame, two flames, three flames. Then he got so sleepy. Nap mats came out, soft and quiet. Miss Ana tucked his blanket in. "Sweet dreams, Victor," she whispered. Victor closed his eyes and held his teddy tight.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Harrison had four little pots on the balcony. He filled each one with smooth, brown dirt. He pushed one carrot seed into each pot. Then he wrote a letter C on the pots with tape.

"Grandma, they are not growing," Harrison said. Two pots had tiny green leaves. Two pots had nothing at all.

Grandma came to look. She pointed at the pots. "Look where the sun is," she said. Harrison looked. The sun was bright on two pots. The wall made a big shadow on the other two.

"The sunny ones grew," Harrison said. "The dark ones did not."

Grandma smiled. "Sun helps seeds grow. Let's move them."

Harrison moved the pots into the sun. He gave each one a drink of water. Every morning he counted them. "One pot, two pots, three pots, four."

One day the dark pots had little leaves too. Harrison pointed at them and jumped up and down.

"Look, Grandma! The sun helped them!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
story:
Joshua wanted to find his red ball. He looked under the bed. He looked behind the chair. The ball was not there.

Then he heard a loud sound outside. "Woof, woof!" The dog next door began to bark. Joshua jumped. His tummy felt tight. His hands felt cold. He was scared of the big sound.

Grandpa came outside with him. "Let's look at the dog," said Grandpa. They stood by the fence. The dog barked one more time. Then Grandpa clapped his hands softly. The dog sat down. It wagged its tail. "He barked because he wanted to say hello," said Grandpa. Joshua felt his tummy loosen. He was not scared now. He laughed, and the dog looked happy too.

Grandpa pointed at the grass. There was the red ball! Joshua felt so excited. He hugged Grandpa. "The dog barked, so we came out," said Joshua. "Then I found my ball." He threw the ball high in the air. "That was cool!" he said.
